outcome: Since 26 January 2024 the conjecture has been refuted in preprint form, none of it yet peer reviewed or formally verified. Putman (arXiv:2608.10012, 8 Aug 2026) gives an explicit 112-vertex bridgeless cubic graph with no Petersen colouring, certified by SAT with DRAT proofs; Jooken (arXiv:2608.10028 v1, 9 Aug 2026) gives a human-checkable proof for that same graph; Goedgebeur, Jooken, Máčajová, Mattiolo and Mazzuoccolo post two 52-vertex counterexamples and an infinite family (Zenodo, 14 Aug 2026; six-author arXiv v3, 11 Sep 2026, adds a hand proof and an order-40 lower bound); and a 68-vertex counterexample was announced on X on 23 Jul 2026, which I could not reach.
problem_asks: One universal claim, as the bullet words it: (a) every bridgeless cubic graph G (hypotheses: bridgeless and cubic; no bound on order); (b) G admits a cycle-continuous mapping to the Petersen graph P, that is a map from the edges of G to the edges of P such that the preimage of every binary cycle of P (an edge set with even degree at every vertex) is a binary cycle of G, in the sense of DeVos, Nešetřil and Raspaud as the sources give it. The bullet asks for existence of such a map for each G, not a construction. It does not ask for the minimum order of a counterexample, for a normal 5-edge-colouring (equivalent per the sources, but not the bullet's words), or for the weaker consequences (Fulkerson, cycle double cover, Berge-Fulkerson, five-cycle double cover). The name 'Jaeger's Petersen-coloring conjecture' is the same claim.

events.what_happened: Bryce Putman posts arXiv:2608.10012, 'A 112-Vertex Counterexample to the Petersen Coloring Conjecture' (single version, 8 Aug 2026, 116 KB; arXiv comment 'Computer-assisted proof'; Zenodo record 10.5281/zenodo.21845291 dated 8 Aug 2026, listed as version 1.1.0). It gives an explicit simple bridgeless cubic graph on 112 vertices with no Petersen colouring and hence no normal 5-edge-colouring, identified by a normalised sorted-edge-list SHA-256 digest. It also gives a separately verified, non-isomorphic D3-symmetric 112-vertex example, and says that, with a theorem of Ma, Mattiolo, Steffen and Wolf, infinitely many connected simple bridgeless cubic graphs have no Petersen colouring. The 52-vertex paper's reference list cites this as [29] and [30].
events.revisions: arXiv: v1 only (8 Aug 2026). Zenodo 21845291: current files FINAL_PAPER_v1.1.0.pdf, a 277 MB DRAT proof archive and ancillary zips; the date of v1.1.0 is not shown on the page I read. The Breakthrough Tracker (secondary) gives 'August 8-14' for the 112-vertex manuscripts.
events.delivers: Refutes the universal claim in the bullet: a bridgeless cubic graph with no Petersen colouring. For cubic graphs the sources state the equivalence with a cycle-continuous map to P (the 52-vertex paper's introduction cites DeVos, Nesetril and Raspaud; MathWorld agrees); I did not check that theorem at source. Restriction: one graph of order 112 (plus the D3-symmetric second graph). Non-colourability is established by computer, not by a human argument in this preprint: the arXiv abstract summary I read reports SAT instances returning UNSAT, certified with DRAT proofs; the Zenodo record names 'SAT encodings' and 'checked DRAT proof certificates' and does not name the solver. The solver name (CaDiCaL, reported as 3.0.1; drat-trim) comes from a summary of the arXiv abstract page, not from a page I read in full.
events.remains: Nothing else in the bullet, which is a single universal claim answered negatively here. Not asked by the bullet and left open by this event: the minimum order of a counterexample (the 52-vertex paper gives 40 to 52 as the range) and whether a counterexample with cyclic edge-connectivity at least 5 exists (MathWorld lists this as open).

checked_by.who: Jorik Jooken (co-author of the later 52-vertex paper; KU Leuven affiliation on Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.21933786)
checked_by.qualification: Named combinatorics researcher and co-author of the 52-vertex work; no other qualification found in the sources
checked_by.what_they_did: Wrote a short human-checkable proof that this same graph has no Petersen colouring, reducing the contradiction to a structural property of the line graph of the Petersen graph, without the large SAT computation (arXiv:2608.10028 v1, 9 Aug 2026; see the Jooken event)

machine_checked.system: SAT (CaDiCaL, reported as 3.0.1 in an arXiv abstract summary) with DRAT proofs checked by drat-trim; the Zenodo record names SAT encodings and checked DRAT certificates

events.directly_checkable: The graph is explicit (112 vertices, 168 edges by cubicity; edge list in the Zenodo ancillary archive, identified by a SHA-256 digest). Non-colourability can be re-run with the SAT encodings and DRAT certificates; I did not download the archive. Jooken's preprint gives a hand argument for the same graph (see its event).
events.doubts: Not peer reviewed; the Zenodo record says it 'has not yet undergone peer review'. Non-colourability rests on a SAT computation (Jooken's v1 abstract gives an instance with 3640 variables and 68324 clauses) whose encoding and certificates I did not check. The Breakthrough Tracker describes the result as 'independently corroborated' but does not name the check; the only candidate I found is Jooken's preprint, by a co-author of the 52-vertex work. The 52-vertex paper's introduction says Putman's result was obtained 'with the use of an AI model' (see ai below).
events.direction: Against the bullet: it exhibits a bridgeless cubic graph with no Petersen colouring, which by the cited equivalence has no cycle-continuous map to the Petersen graph, so it is a counterexample to the universal claim.
events.object: An explicit simple connected bridgeless cubic graph on 112 vertices (168 edges), identified by a normalised sorted-edge-list SHA-256 digest. Per the arXiv abstract summary, it is built from three copies of a four-pole L and a claw six-pole C, where L is built from four copies of a four-pole F (the Petersen graph with the two endpoints of one edge deleted) and one copy of C. The arXiv abstract states it has no Petersen colouring and hence no normal 5-edge-colouring; the non-colourability is shown by UNSAT instances. Girth five is per a search summary of the paper, not confirmed on the page I read. The object is explicit; the non-colourability is computer-verified, not a non-constructive existence proof. Also a non-isomorphic D3-symmetric 112-vertex graph with a separate verification. Whether this contradicts the bullet is for the judging pass.
people: Bryce Putman (listed as an independent researcher on Zenodo)

systems.name: OpenAI language-model systems
systems.what_it_did: The authors say the systems were used 'extensively in the discovery, computational search, verification, and preparation of this work'. The paper does not say which step produced the graph, or which model. The author 'reviewed the final claims and artifacts and accepts responsibility for the contents'. The six-author paper's introduction describes Putman's counterexamples as obtained 'with the use of an AI model'.
systems.basis_quote: OpenAI language-model systems were used extensively in the discovery, computational search, verification, and preparation of this work.

events.what_happened: Jorik Jooken, sole author, posts arXiv:2608.10028 v1 (9 Aug 2026), titled 'A human-checkable proof of the 112-vertex counterexample to the Petersen coloring conjecture'. Its abstract: Putman's 112-vertex graph was verified non-colourable by a SAT instance with 3640 variables and 68324 clauses; 'We give a short human-checkable proof that this graph is indeed a counterexample', determining the colouring behaviour of the multipoles by explicit finite case analyses and reducing the final contradiction to a structural property of the line graph of the Petersen graph. v2 (14 Aug 2026) is marked 'a preliminary version of the paper'; its comment says a forthcoming version will also present a 52-vertex counterexample and an infinite family of girth-5 counterexamples. v3 (11 Sep 2026) and v4 (30 Sep 2026) are the six-author paper (see that event), retitled.
events.revisions: v1 9 Aug 2026 (sole author, 12 KB); v2 14 Aug 2026 (same title, 'preliminary'); v3 11 Sep 2026 (six authors, retitled, 235 KB); v4 30 Sep 2026 (246 KB).
events.delivers: A hand (non-SAT) proof that Putman's 112-vertex graph has no Petersen colouring. Restriction: the same one graph of order 112 as the Putman event. It adds an independent route to the same negative answer, and no new counterexample.
events.remains: Same as the Putman event: nothing else in the bullet; the minimum order and the cyclic-edge-connectivity question are not asked and not settled here.
events.directly_checkable: The proof is meant to be read by hand: finite case analyses of multipole colourings, then a structural argument about the line graph of the Petersen graph. I could not read the PDF body (the fetch tool could not decode its streams), so I have not checked any step of it.
events.doubts: Preliminary and unrefereed (v2 says so). I did not read the proof body, so I cannot say whether the case analyses are complete. I found no third-party reading of this proof in any source. The tracker's 'independently corroborated' label does not name a reader beyond the author.
events.direction: Against the bullet, in the same direction as the Putman event: it argues by hand that Putman's graph is a counterexample to the universal claim.
events.object: No new object: the 112-vertex graph of the Putman event.

events.what_happened: On X, the account NeuralReformist announced a 68-vertex counterexample to Jaeger's conjecture and supplied an encoded graph. MathWorld dates the post to 23 July 2026 and says it credits GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra; the six-author paper's introduction says: 'A counterexample on 68 vertices to Conjecture 1, credited to GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra, was posted on X in July 2026.' The day is from MathWorld alone. The post itself could not be fetched (x.com returned HTTP 402), so its wording and graph were not read.
events.delivers: If the encoded graph is correct, a bridgeless cubic graph of order 68 with no Petersen colouring, which is a counterexample to the universal claim. I did not verify it, and no independent verification appears in any source I read.
events.remains: Same as the Putman event. MathWorld notes that neither this announcement nor the Putman one determines the minimum possible order.
events.directly_checkable: Only with the encoded graph, which I did not obtain. The six-author paper says the 68-vertex graph (with the 52- and 112-vertex ones) can be obtained from House of Graphs by searching for 'Petersen Coloring'; I did not check House of Graphs.
events.doubts: No account by the announcer was reached. The announcement is a single unverified post, superseded in the literature by the 112-vertex result. The six-author paper mentions the 68-vertex graph in several sections (normal colourings, Berge-Fulkerson, cycle double covers), and MathWorld reports computer checks of cover properties for it, but I found no check of its non-colourability. The tracker does not mention the 68-vertex graph at all.
events.direction: Against the bullet as announced: a counterexample to the universal claim.
events.object: A 68-vertex graph given in encoded form in the X post (per MathWorld). I did not obtain or inspect it, so its explicitness and its non-colourability are unknown to me.
people: NeuralReformist (X account; identity not established in the sources)

events.what_happened: A five-author Zenodo working paper, 'A smaller counterexample and infinite family of counterexamples to the Petersen Coloring Conjecture' (Goedgebeur, Jooken, Máčajová, Mattiolo, Mazzuoccolo), published 14 Aug 2026 (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21933786, CC BY 4.0). The record's description: a counterexample on 52 vertices, the smallest known; an infinite family of cyclically 4-edge-connected cubic graphs without a Petersen colouring; a first version, with a subsequent version in preparation; Putman's disproof is described as 'computer-assisted verification'. The record says nothing about AI or about how the graphs were found. The arXiv v2 of Jooken's preprint (14 Aug) announces the same results as forthcoming and links a Zenodo DOI ending 21933785, which I did not open.
events.revisions: Zenodo version 1 (14 Aug 2026), file manuscript_infinite_family_counterexamples_petersen_coloring_conjecture.pdf (251.4 kB). The same work continues as arXiv:2608.10028 v3 (11 Sep) and v4 (30 Sep); see the next event.
events.delivers: A counterexample on 52 vertices to the universal claim (the later arXiv text has two such graphs), plus an infinite family of girth-5 cyclically 4-edge-connected counterexamples. Restriction: the Zenodo description does not give the order range of the family; the later text gives every even order at least 60. I could not read the PDF body, so I cannot say whether the 14 Aug version already contained the theoretical proof of non-colourability.
events.directly_checkable: The 52-vertex graph is explicit (construction described in the later arXiv text; see the next event). I did not verify it.
events.doubts: A working paper, not peer reviewed. The Breakthrough Tracker (secondary) describes the smaller graph as independently unchecked in its 1 Sep 2026 note. The author list here has five names (no Ulyanov); the arXiv v3 and v4 list six. The arXiv v2 comment cites Zenodo DOI 21933785 for the same forthcoming results, while the record I opened is 21933786; I could not reconcile the two.
events.direction: Against the bullet: a 52-vertex bridgeless cubic counterexample, as described.
events.object: Two cubic graphs of order 52 described as having no Petersen colouring (construction in the next event), and an infinite family described as cyclically 4-edge-connected. The non-colourability is claimed by a theoretical argument.

events.what_happened: arXiv:2608.10028 v3 (11 Sep 2026) and v4 (30 Sep 2026): six authors (Goedgebeur, Jooken, Máčajová, Mattiolo, Mazzuoccolo, Ulyanov), retitled 'Disproving the Petersen Coloring Conjecture: Theoretical Analysis and an Infinite Family of Counterexamples'. The v3 abstract, read in pieces: 'two counterexamples of order 52, currently the smallest known, and provide a purely theoretical proof'; an infinite family of cyclically 4-edge-connected cubic graphs without a Petersen colouring 'for every even order at least 60'; 'through computational verification, we show that any counterexample must have order at least 40'; and that the counterexamples answer related problems negatively. The v4 text, as extracted by a tool (paraphrased where not quoted), gives the construction: three copies of a 5-pole F (17 vertices each) joined cyclically, plus one central vertex; the second graph is obtained by switching two edges. Non-colourability is Theorem 6: two constraints on the three middle edges and the blue/red matching between consecutive F-copies, eliminated by a case analysis of nine configurations (Lemma 5). The infinite family replaces a copy of a four-pole W by one of four four-poles M1 to M4, giving orders 60, 62, 64, 66 and then all even orders by induction (adding 8 vertices). The text says Lemma 7 was verified with computer assistance. The lower bound uses the complete list of weak snarks on 38 vertices supplied by Gunnar Brinkmann and Steven Van Overberghe (7,142,217,899 graphs; about 12 CPU years).
events.revisions: arXiv v1 (9 Aug, Jooken alone, 112-vertex proof); v2 (14 Aug, Jooken alone, preliminary, announces 52-vertex result); v3 (11 Sep 2026, six authors, retitled, 235 KB); v4 (30 Sep 2026, 246 KB). The tracker gives the 52-vertex addition as a '2026-09-01' revision; that does not match the arXiv or Zenodo dates and I found no source for 1 Sep.
events.delivers: (i) Two explicit cubic graphs of order 52 with no Petersen colouring, so counterexamples to the universal claim, with non-colourability proved by hand (Theorem 6, per the v4 text as extracted). (ii) An infinite family, for each even order at least 60, of cyclically 4-edge-connected counterexamples of girth 5 (per the same text). (iii) A computational lower bound: no counterexample of order at most 38, hence order at least 40. Restrictions: (iii) is a computer enumeration and does not bear on the bullet's universal claim, which does not ask for minimum order; (i) and (ii) depend on the hand argument and the explicit construction.
events.remains: Nothing in the universal claim: answered negatively. Not asked by the bullet and left open: the exact minimum order (40 to 52 per MathWorld and the record), and whether a counterexample with cyclic edge-connectivity at least 5 exists (MathWorld: open).

machine_checked.system: custom computer enumeration over the 38-vertex weak-snark list (software not named in the text I read); Lemma 7 'verified with computer assistance'

events.directly_checkable: The two 52-vertex graphs are explicit (construction above). The non-colourability argument is a finite case analysis over nine configurations, which a reader could check by hand; I did not check it. The order-40 bound is not hand-checkable.
events.doubts: (1) Not peer reviewed; the tracker calls the 52-vertex manuscript an unrefereed first version and says it gives no separate machine-checkable certificate. (2) The order-40 bound rests on an exhaustive computation over a list supplied by others, and no certificate is described. (3) Sources disagree on the bound: the arXiv text says 40; the tracker says a 38-vertex lower bound from earlier work. (4) The author list changed across versions (Ulyanov on arXiv v3 and v4, absent from the 14 Aug Zenodo record). (5) Lemma 7 uses computer assistance. None of these is a specific error I found; they are the points a careful reader would check.
events.direction: Against the bullet: two 52-vertex counterexamples and an infinite family. The authors frame the results as negative answers to the conjecture and to several related problems.
events.object: Two cyclically 4-edge-connected cubic graphs of order 52 with no Petersen colouring: three copies of a 5-pole F of 17 vertices joined cyclically, plus one central vertex; the second graph obtained by switching two edges in the first. The v4 text says all graphs in the paper have girth 5 and cyclic edge-connectivity 4. Also an explicit infinite family, one graph for each even order at least 60, built by replacing four-pole copies. These are explicit constructions; non-colourability is shown by the hand argument, not by a computer search.

events.what_happened: Brinkmann, Goedgebeur, Hägglund and Markström, 'Generation and Properties of Snarks', arXiv:1206.6690 (28 Jun 2012; J. Combin. Theory Ser. B, 2013). They generate all non-isomorphic snarks on up to 36 vertices and report that Jaeger's Petersen colouring conjecture holds for all snarks of these orders.
events.revisions: v1 28 Jun 2012; published JCTB 2013 (DOI 10.1016/j.jctb.2013.05.001, per the arXiv page).
events.delivers: The conjecture holds for every snark on at most 36 vertices. This is a finite check over snarks; bridgeless cubic graphs that are 3-edge-colourable satisfy the conjecture trivially (Šámal's comment, see the 2011 event). It does not move the universal claim for larger orders.
events.remains: The universal claim for every order above 36.

checked_by.who: Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series B (referees not named in the sources I read)
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper in JCTB 2013 (per the journal reference on the arXiv page). Publication does not itself verify the computation.

machine_checked.system: the authors' custom snark-generation program (not named on the abstract page)

events.direction: Consistent with the universal claim at orders up to 36; no counterexample of those orders.

events.what_happened: A comment on the Open Problem Garden page for the conjecture, by Robert Šámal (24 Nov 2011), says the conjecture is trivially true for 3-edge-colourable graphs, and reports a computer check, using lists of snarks, of all graphs up to 34 vertices, plus flower snarks.
events.delivers: An informal, reported computer check of the conjecture for all graphs up to 34 vertices. Finite orders only. Superseded in scope by the 2012 snark enumeration to order 36.
events.remains: The universal claim for all orders.
events.doubts: An informal comment; I found no write-up or code. The comment does not say which snark lists were used.
events.direction: Consistent with the universal claim at orders up to 34.

events.what_happened: Vahan V. Mkrtchyan, 'A remark on Petersen coloring conjecture of Jaeger', arXiv:1201.4472 (21 Jan 2012; v2 24 Jul 2012); Australas. J. Combin. 56 (2013) 145-151. It shows that if a connected bridgeless cubic graph G satisfies G ≺ P (P is coloured by the edges of G), then G = P; it also introduces the Sylvester coloring conjecture.
events.revisions: v1 21 Jan 2012; v2 24 Jul 2012; journal reference AJC 56 (2013) 145-151.
events.delivers: A result in the reverse direction: among connected bridgeless cubic graphs, only P itself admits the colouring relation with P as the colouring graph (G ≺ P). The bullet asks the other direction (P ≺ G for every bridgeless cubic G), so this does not bear on it.
events.remains: The bullet's direction, P ≺ G for every bridgeless cubic G.

checked_by.who: Australasian Journal of Combinatorics (referees not named in the sources I read)
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper in AJC 56 (2013) (per the journal reference on the arXiv page)

events.direction: Neutral for the bullet: it classifies the reverse relation, and does not decide the bullet's direction.

events.what_happened: François Pirot, Jean-Sébastien Sereni and Riste Škrekovski, 'Variations on the Petersen colouring conjecture', arXiv:1905.07913 (20 May 2019); Electron. J. Combin. 27(1) (2020) P1.8.
events.delivers: A weaker, variant result: every bridgeless cubic graph has a 4-edge-colouring in which at most a 4/5 fraction of the edges fail the condition; the bound is tight (the Petersen graph is the only connected graph where it cannot be lowered). It is not a P-colouring of every bridgeless cubic graph.

checked_by.who: Electronic Journal of Combinatorics (referees not named in the sources I read)

events.direction: Neutral to the bullet: a partial variant that stops short of a P-colouring.

events.what_happened: Ligang Jin and Yingli Kang, 'Partially normal 5-edge-colorings of cubic graphs', arXiv:1911.06759 (15 Nov 2019). Every bridgeless cubic graph has a proper 5-edge-colouring with at least |E(G)| − μ3(G) normal edges, which is at least 4/5 of the edges; it improves earlier results by Bílková and Šámal. No journal reference listed.
events.revisions: v1 15 Nov 2019; the comments note an earlier version in the first author's Paderborn dissertation.
events.delivers: A partial result: a proper 5-edge-colouring in which at least 4/5 of the edges are normal. The conjecture asks for all edges normal, so this stops short.
events.remains: The full claim (all edges normal, equivalently a P-colouring).
events.direction: Neutral to the bullet: partial, via a weaker normal-edge count.

events.what_happened: Davide Mattiolo, Giuseppe Mazzuoccolo and Vahan Mkrtchyan, 'On sublinear approximations for the Petersen coloring conjecture', arXiv:2104.09241 (19 Apr 2021). They show the conjecture is equivalent to the existence of a sublinear function f such that every bridgeless cubic graph has a proper 5-edge-colouring with at most f(|V|) abnormal edges, and for k = 2, 3, 4 an analogous statement for k-edge-connected cubic graphs is equivalent to a bound of 2k+1 abnormal edges. No journal reference listed.
events.delivers: A reformulation with partial corollaries for k-edge-connected classes. It does not establish a P-colouring for any new graph class.
events.direction: Neutral to the bullet: an equivalent reformulation, plus partial results on k-edge-connected graphs.

events.what_happened: Yulai Ma, Davide Mattiolo, Eckhard Steffen and Isaak H. Wolf, 'Sets of r-graphs that color all r-graphs', arXiv:2305.08619 (15 May 2023). The paper defines H_r, an inclusion-wise minimal set of connected r-graphs that colours every connected r-graph, shows it is unique, and characterises its members; it discusses the Petersen Coloring Conjecture, stated in the abstract as 'the Petersen graph P colors every bridgeless cubic graph'. A search summary of a 2026 preprint says the paper shows the conjecture is equivalent to H_3 = {P}, and that otherwise H_3 is infinite; I did not confirm this in the abstract I read.
events.revisions: v1 15 May 2023 (25 pages, 7 figures). The same authors' Combinatorica 44 (2024) paper is a different result (on m(t, r)) and is not this event.
events.delivers: A structural reformulation (the minimal colouring family H_r), not a colouring result for any new cubic graph. Per the summary of the later preprint, it makes the conjecture equivalent to H_3 = {P}, so the 'infinitely many' statement in the 112-vertex paper follows only if the conjecture is false.
events.doubts: The H_3 characterisation is second-hand (search summary); I read only the abstract of the arXiv paper.
events.direction: Neutral to the bullet: a reformulation.

events.what_happened: Jelena Sedlar and Riste Škrekovski, 'Normal 5-edge coloring of some more snarks superpositioned by the Petersen graph', arXiv:2312.08739 (14 Dec 2023; v2 15 Dec 2023). They consider superpositions of snarks along a cycle with the Petersen graph, cover the remaining connection types not handled in their earlier paper, and conclude that the Petersen Coloring Conjecture holds for all of them. No journal reference listed; the page mentions an earlier paper by the same authors in Applied Mathematics and Computation 467 (2024), which I did not locate.
events.delivers: The conjecture for a restricted family: superpositions of snarks with the Petersen graph along a cycle, under the connection types the paper covers. The bullet's universal claim is not reached.
events.remains: All bridgeless cubic graphs outside those families.
events.direction: Consistent with the universal claim on a restricted family.

events.what_happened: Igor Fabrici, Borut Lužar, Roman Soták and Diana Švecová, 'Normal 6-edge-colorings of cubic graphs with oddness 2', arXiv:2508.20565 (28 Aug 2025). They prove that every cubic graph with oddness 2 has a normal edge-colouring with at most 6 colours. No journal reference listed.
events.revisions: v1 28 Aug 2025 (per the arXiv page I read).
events.delivers: A weaker bound (6 colours, one more than the conjecture's 5) for one class of cubic graphs (oddness 2). It is a neighbouring result on the normal-colouring formulation and does not show the 5-colour bound for any graph.
events.remains: The 5-colour claim for every bridgeless cubic graph, and the universal P-colouring claim.
events.direction: Neutral to the bullet: a weaker neighbouring bound for a restricted class.

events.what_happened: Isaak H. Wolf, 'A counterexample to the S10- and the S12-Conjecture', arXiv:2509.14184 (17 Sep 2025; 6 pages, submitted for publication). It gives a small counterexample to two conjectures of Mkrtchyan and coauthors: that every cubic graph has an S10-colouring, and that every cubic graph with a perfect matching has an S12-colouring. The abstract says the work is 'Motivated by the Petersen Coloring Conjecture'.
events.revisions: v1 17 Sep 2025 (per the arXiv page I read).
events.delivers: A counterexample to the S10 and S12 colouring conjectures, which are different colouring problems (colourings by the Sylvester graph, not the Petersen graph). It does not refute, or prove, the Petersen claim.
events.directly_checkable: The counterexample is small; I did not check it.
events.direction: Neutral to the bullet: a counterexample to different conjectures motivated by the Petersen conjecture.
events.object: A small cubic graph with a perfect matching having no S10-colouring (per the abstract), which also defeats the S12 conjecture. I did not inspect it.

events.what_happened: A proof of the Cycle Double Cover Conjecture attributed to OpenAI (a three-page PDF, reported as posted 10 Jul 2026; the reports say the proof was produced by GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra). Jim Geelen's expository note on it, arXiv:2607.15399 'OpenAI's proof of the Cycle Double Cover Theorem' (16 Jul 2026), attributes the proof to OpenAI. The 52-vertex paper's section 5.5 cites it as an OpenAI preprint. The OpenAI PDF could not be decoded by my fetch tool. The 10 Jul date and the GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra attribution come from news aggregators, not the PDF.
events.revisions: Expository notes by Geelen (16 Jul 2026) and by Oum (not opened). Per aggregators, a later revision or a Codex write-up is mentioned; not verified.
events.delivers: A proof of the Cycle Double Cover Conjecture as reported. This is a different problem: the Petersen claim implies cycle double covers, not the reverse, so a proof of the cycle double cover conjecture does not establish a cycle-continuous map from every bridgeless cubic graph to P.

checked_by.who: Jim Geelen (sole author of the expository note arXiv:2607.15399)
checked_by.what_they_did: Wrote a note explaining the OpenAI argument, which builds on Jaeger's nowhere-zero flow result; the note says it 'offers no new insights'

events.doubts: The OpenAI PDF was not readable to me; the attribution to GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra is second-hand. Aggregators disagree on whether the proof is machine-verified. No journal acceptance found.
events.direction: Neutral to the bullet: a proof of a consequence of the conjecture, not of the conjecture.
people: OpenAI (attributed; the human contributors are not named in the sources I read)

disputes.summary: The 68-vertex announcement (23 Jul 2026, credited to GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra, not verified by me) precedes Putman's 112-vertex preprint (8 Aug 2026), which the tracker and MathWorld treat as the first verified refutation. The six-author paper calls Putman's result 'independent' and does not dispute the 68-vertex claim. I found no competing priority claim beyond this sequence.

summary: The bullet is refuted in preprints dated after 26 January 2024, and none of the refuting papers is yet peer reviewed or formally verified. The first verified counterexample is Putman's 112-vertex graph (arXiv:2608.10012 and Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.21845291, 8 Aug 2026), whose non-colourability is a SAT computation certified by DRAT proofs; Putman's own text says 'OpenAI language-model systems were used extensively in the discovery, computational search, verification, and preparation of this work', which names no model and does not say what the systems did at the discovery step. Jooken's single-author preprint (arXiv:2608.10028 v1, 9 Aug 2026) gives a hand proof for the same graph; its v2 declaration (14 Aug) says the author used 'ChatGPT (OpenAI, GPT-5.6 Sol)' for 'proofreading, improving the presentation and rewriting parts of the proofs, as well as ... figures and tables', and that 'All mathematical statements, arguments, and proofs in this paper were independently verified by the author'. I did not put that system in ai.systems, because the uses listed are write-up and checking, but it is the closest call in this record: if the rewriting changed a step of the hand proof, the later pass should count it. The 52-vertex result first appears in a five-author Zenodo record of 14 Aug 2026 (10.5281/zenodo.21933786), and in six-author arXiv v3 of 11 Sep 2026, which adds a hand proof (Theorem 6, as extracted from v4), an infinite family for every even order at least 60, and a computer lower bound of 40 on the order of any counterexample. That paper's only AI statement is 'The role of AI in this work was restricted to independently double-checking the accuracy of the properties of the multipoles under consideration', and it refers to 'an AI model' for Putman's work and to 'GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra' for the 68-vertex announcement. The 68-vertex graph was announced on X on 23 Jul 2026 (day per MathWorld only); the post returned HTTP 402 and the graph was not obtained, so it stands as an unverified announcement with no authors' own account of its AI role. Source disagreements: the Breakthrough Tracker dates the 52-vertex addition to 1 Sep 2026 (no source for that date; Zenodo is 14 Aug, arXiv v3 11 Sep), gives 38 as the lower bound where the paper gives 40, and paraphrases Jooken's AI sentence in terms the primary text does not use; the arXiv v2 comment links Zenodo DOI 21933785 while the record I opened is 21933786. Pre-2024 events are all partial, restricted or reformulations: all snarks to order 36 (2012), superpositions of snarks (Dec 2023), weaker colouring variants (2019), and equivalent reformulations (2021, 2023); a 2025 normal 6-colouring result and a 2025 counterexample to the S10 and S12 conjectures are neighbours on other colourings. The OpenAI cycle-double-cover proof (July 2026) is a different problem and is recorded as such. The judgement that the bullet's universal claim is refuted rests on the reading that, for cubic G, a P-colouring is equivalent to a cycle-continuous map to P, which the sources state (citing DeVos, Nesetril and Raspaud) and which I did not check at source.
competing_reading: Against 'refuted': both counterexamples are unrefereed preprints, the 112-vertex non-colourability is computer-verified, and the hand proof of that graph (Jooken, v2) is preliminary and I could not read its body; on a strict reading of 'verified', the bullet's status is still in doubt until either the SAT certificates or the hand proof is checked by a third party, although the 52-vertex result also has a hand proof (unrefereed, body unread by me). Against 'AI did the mathematics': the authors' own AI sentences are 'discovery, computational search, verification, and preparation' (Putman, unnamed model), 'proofreading ... rewriting parts of the proofs ... figures and tables' (Jooken, ChatGPT), and 'double-checking' (six authors); none says a model supplied a mathematical idea, and the 112-vertex graph's human-designed encoding and the hand proof of it are the mathematics a reader would credit to people. Against counting the 68-vertex event at all: no account from its announcer was reached, and the only AI attribution is secondhand.
what_would_settle_it: (1) Peer review, or an independent re-run, of the 112-vertex SAT instances and DRAT certificates (Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.21845291), and of Jooken's hand proof (arXiv:2608.10028 v1/v2), including its full text. (2) Putman's, or the author group's, dated account of what the named or unnamed AI systems produced in the discovery of the 112-vertex graph, and of whether any AI-written proof text changed a mathematical step in Jooken's proof. (3) The NeuralReformist post or its encoded 68-vertex graph, and an independent check of its non-colourability. (4) The full text of arXiv:2608.10028 v3 or v4 (PDF), confirming Theorem 6, Lemma 7 and the order-40 computation, and the 38-vertex weak-snark list used. (5) Resolving whether Zenodo 21933785 (cited by arXiv v2) or 21933786 (opened here) holds the 52-vertex paper, and whether the 14 Aug version already contained the non-colourability proof. (6) Confirmation at source of the cubic equivalence between P-colourings and cycle-continuous maps (DeVos, Nesetril, Raspaud).

event.what_happened: Bryce Putman posts arXiv:2608.10012, 'A 112-Vertex Counterexample to the Petersen Coloring Conjecture' (single version, 8 Aug 2026, 116 KB; arXiv comment 'Computer-assisted proof'; Zenodo record 10.5281/zenodo.21845291 dated 8 Aug 2026, listed as version 1.1.0). It gives an explicit simple bridgeless cubic graph on 112 vertices with no Petersen colouring and hence no normal 5-edge-colouring, identified by a normalised sorted-edge-list SHA-256 digest. It also gives a separately verified, non-isomorphic D3-symmetric 112-vertex example, and says that, with a theorem of Ma, Mattiolo, Steffen and Wolf, infinitely many connected simple bridgeless cubic graphs have no Petersen colouring. The 52-vertex paper's reference list cites this as [29] and [30].
event.revisions: arXiv: v1 only (8 Aug 2026). Zenodo 21845291: current files FINAL_PAPER_v1.1.0.pdf, a 277 MB DRAT proof archive and ancillary zips; the date of v1.1.0 is not shown on the page I read. The Breakthrough Tracker (secondary) gives 'August 8-14' for the 112-vertex manuscripts.
event.delivers: Refutes the universal claim in the bullet: a bridgeless cubic graph with no Petersen colouring. For cubic graphs the sources state the equivalence with a cycle-continuous map to P (the 52-vertex paper's introduction cites DeVos, Nesetril and Raspaud; MathWorld agrees); I did not check that theorem at source. Restriction: one graph of order 112 (plus the D3-symmetric second graph). Non-colourability is established by computer, not by a human argument in this preprint: the arXiv abstract summary I read reports SAT instances returning UNSAT, certified with DRAT proofs; the Zenodo record names 'SAT encodings' and 'checked DRAT proof certificates' and does not name the solver. The solver name (CaDiCaL, reported as 3.0.1; drat-trim) comes from a summary of the arXiv abstract page, not from a page I read in full.
event.remains: Nothing else in the bullet, which is a single universal claim answered negatively here. Not asked by the bullet and left open by this event: the minimum order of a counterexample (the 52-vertex paper gives 40 to 52 as the range) and whether a counterexample with cyclic edge-connectivity at least 5 exists (MathWorld lists this as open).

event.directly_checkable: The graph is explicit (112 vertices, 168 edges by cubicity; edge list in the Zenodo ancillary archive, identified by a SHA-256 digest). Non-colourability can be re-run with the SAT encodings and DRAT certificates; I did not download the archive. Jooken's preprint gives a hand argument for the same graph (see its event).
event.doubts: Not peer reviewed; the Zenodo record says it 'has not yet undergone peer review'. Non-colourability rests on a SAT computation (Jooken's v1 abstract gives an instance with 3640 variables and 68324 clauses) whose encoding and certificates I did not check. The Breakthrough Tracker describes the result as 'independently corroborated' but does not name the check; the only candidate I found is Jooken's preprint, by a co-author of the 52-vertex work. The 52-vertex paper's introduction says Putman's result was obtained 'with the use of an AI model' (see ai below).
event.direction: Against the bullet: it exhibits a bridgeless cubic graph with no Petersen colouring, which by the cited equivalence has no cycle-continuous map to the Petersen graph, so it is a counterexample to the universal claim.
event.object: An explicit simple connected bridgeless cubic graph on 112 vertices (168 edges), identified by a normalised sorted-edge-list SHA-256 digest. Per the arXiv abstract summary, it is built from three copies of a four-pole L and a claw six-pole C, where L is built from four copies of a four-pole F (the Petersen graph with the two endpoints of one edge deleted) and one copy of C. The arXiv abstract states it has no Petersen colouring and hence no normal 5-edge-colouring; the non-colourability is shown by UNSAT instances. Girth five is per a search summary of the paper, not confirmed on the page I read. The object is explicit; the non-colourability is computer-verified, not a non-constructive existence proof. Also a non-isomorphic D3-symmetric 112-vertex graph with a separate verification. Whether this contradicts the bullet is for the judging pass.

judgement.why: The statement makes one universal claim, so a single explicit bridgeless cubic graph with no Petersen colouring answers all of it (scope whole, counterexample, refuted), given the cubic equivalence between P-colourings and cycle-continuous maps that the sources state. Putman's 112-vertex graph counts as digested: Jooken, a named combinatorialist who did not write Putman's paper, published a separate hand proof that this same graph is non-colourable, and that is a verification by a third party. Jooken's own preprint, the 52-vertex Zenodo record and the arXiv v3 have no outside reader yet, so they are unreviewed. Putman's AI role was the close call. The authors' own sentence lists 'discovery' and 'computational search' among what the OpenAI systems were used for, which goes beyond checking or writing and means the systems contributed to finding the graph. But it does not say the model produced the graph, and a human author designed and took responsibility for the work, so I answered assisted rather than generated. Jooken's ChatGPT use (proofreading, rewriting, figures) is not in ai.systems and is write-up work, so I answered none. The 68-vertex announcement's credit to GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra is second-hand and its ai.systems is empty, so I answered none and doubtful. Every event before the snapshot either checks finitely many graphs, settles a changed question, reformulates the problem, or covers a restricted family (Sedlar–Škrekovski, case).
judgement.doubts: Putman's assisted (not generated) rests on a vague provenance sentence; an account from the author of who found the graph could raise it to generated. Digestion of Putman's graph relies on Jooken's hand proof, whose body the researcher did not read; Jooken is also a co-author of the competing 52-vertex work. The 68-vertex X post may be credited to GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra, but that credit could not be confirmed at source. The cycle-continuous equivalence was not checked at source.
